pillar: Head and Neck and Oral Cancer Treatment in India

items.q: How much does oral cancer treatment cost in India?
items.a: Oral cancer treatment in India usually costs between USD 4,000 and USD 12,000, depending on the stage and the plan. Surgery with reconstruction sits at the higher end, while radiotherapy alone sits lower. Robotic surgery, PET-CT scans, and immunotherapy drugs add to the total. Most quotes cover surgeon fees, hospital stay, and standard tests. Prices vary between hospitals and cities, so ask for a written estimate before you travel.

items.q: Why do so many patients come to India for head and neck cancer treatment?
items.a: India treats more oral cancer than almost any country in the world, so its surgeons operate on these tumours daily. Tata Memorial Centre alone sees thousands of head and neck cases each year. That volume builds skill in free-flap reconstruction, robotic surgery, and organ preservation. Treatment often begins within one to two weeks of arrival. Outcomes still depend on your stage and general health, so results vary from person to person.

items.q: How long will I need to stay in India for treatment?
items.a: Plan for six to ten weeks if your treatment includes surgery followed by radiotherapy. Surgery alone usually needs three to four weeks, including recovery and stitch removal. A full radiotherapy course runs six to seven weeks of daily weekday sessions, and chemoradiation adds weekly infusion days. Your team may extend the stay if wound healing is slow or a feeding tube is needed, so keep your visa dates flexible.

items.q: Will I be able to speak and eat normally after surgery?
items.a: Most patients regain speech and swallowing, but how much depends on how much tissue is removed and from where. Small tongue or cheek tumours often heal with near-normal function. Larger removals need reconstruction using tissue from your forearm, thigh, or leg, plus speech and swallowing therapy for several months. A temporary feeding tube is common. Ask your surgeon to describe the expected change in function before you consent, since recovery varies widely.

items.q: Is robotic surgery available for throat cancer in India?
items.a: Yes, transoral robotic surgery is offered at major Indian cancer centres in Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad. It reaches tonsil and tongue-base tumours through the mouth, avoiding a jaw-splitting incision, which often means less pain and faster swallowing recovery. It suits selected early and intermediate tumours rather than bulky ones. Eligibility depends on tumour size, site, and how wide you can open your mouth, so a specialist assessment comes first.

items.q: What is the difference between IMRT and proton therapy for head and neck cancer?
items.a: IMRT shapes X-ray beams around the tumour and is the standard radiotherapy for head and neck cancer in India. Proton therapy stops inside the target, sparing more of the salivary glands, spinal cord, and swallowing muscles. Protons are available at one centre in Chennai and cost several times more. For many tumours IMRT gives comparable control, so proton therapy is usually reserved for selected cases like skull base tumours or re-treatment.

items.q: Do I need a medical visa, and how do I arrange the hospital?
items.a: You need an Indian medical visa, which requires an invitation letter from the treating hospital along with your reports. Two family members can travel on medical attendant visas. Most hospitals issue the letter within a few days once their tumour board reviews your scans and biopsy. CancerFax can help pass your records to Indian head and neck teams for an opinion and an estimate, though the hospital and the embassy decide admission and visa approval.

items.q: Can I still be treated if my cancer has spread or come back?
items.a: Yes, treatment options exist for recurrent and metastatic head and neck cancer, though the goal often shifts towards control and comfort rather than cure. Salvage surgery, re-irradiation, immunotherapy with pembrolizumab or nivolumab, and targeted drugs such as cetuximab are all used in India. Clinical trials may also be open to you. Eligibility depends on your earlier treatment, PD-L1 testing, and fitness, so send your full records for review.

items.q: How soon after diagnosis should treatment start?
items.a: Aim to start within four to six weeks of diagnosis, because head and neck tumours can grow quickly and long delays are linked to worse outcomes. Use that window to finish staging scans, a dental check, and a nutrition assessment, all of which prevent problems later. Indian hospitals can often schedule surgery within one to two weeks of arrival. If a wait is unavoidable, ask your oncologist what can safely bridge the gap.

items.q: What follow-up will I need after I go home?
items.a: Expect clinic checks every two to three months for the first two years, then less often, since most recurrences appear early. Each visit includes an examination of the mouth, neck, and throat, with a scan or a scope if something feels wrong. Thyroid blood tests are needed yearly after neck radiotherapy. Your Indian team can share a written follow-up plan with your local doctor, and CancerFax can help keep those reports moving between them.
